standard.title: Ideas That Emerged and Influenced Change
standard.description: the ideas that emerged and influenced change in society, such as nationalism, capitalism, imperialism, socialism, egalitarianism and Chartism
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe significant events and their causes and effects (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K07). They have not yet examined how abstract political and economic ideas — capitalism, socialism, nationalism, Chartism — emerged from specific historical contexts, or how to explain the basis of an idea and identify the changes it produced.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain why an idea emerged and the basis of that idea — including Chartism — and identify changes that arose from it; examine the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights; and examine the role of religious beliefs in movements for reform.

nodes.label: Ideas as historical forces — how ideas emerge from context and produce change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how abstract ideas emerge from specific historical conditions and can identify changes that resulted from them — understanding ideas as historical causes, not just intellectual products.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain that ideas like capitalism or socialism emerged in response to specific historical conditions (industrialisation, poverty, inequality) and describe at least one change produced by each idea.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe capitalism as a systematised defence of private property, free markets and profit — emerging from commercial and industrial expansion; socialism as a critique of capitalism's inequalities — emerging from industrial poverty and exploitation; nationalism as the idea that shared culture/language/ethnicity should be the basis of political community — emerging from the French Revolution and industrialisation's cultural homogenisation; egalitarianism as a challenge to inherited hierarchy — emerging from Enlightenment ideas and colonial social conditions; explain how each idea found expression in specific political movements and reforms.
wider: Examine the intellectual lineages connecting ideas — how did Enlightenment ideas about reason and rights enable both capitalism (Locke, Smith) and socialism (Marx, Owen)? What shared premise did they both build from?
Evaluate which idea had the greatest impact on the modern world — developing a position and anticipating objections
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that ideas have historical contexts and produce historical effects is the conceptual prerequisite for all subsequent nodes. Students who treat ideas as floating intellectual abstractions rather than as historically situated forces cannot explain why specific ideas emerged when they did or why they produced specific changes.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe historical ideas as truths or opinions rather than as historically situated responses to specific conditions. Making the context-idea-effect chain explicit is the scaffold for the whole standard.

success_criteria: Explains how at least two ideas emerged from specific historical conditions
Identifies at least one change produced by each idea

nodes.label: Chartism — a case study in popular political ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why Chartism emerged, describe the basis of its demands, and identify the changes that arose from the Chartist movement.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the People's Charter's main demands (universal male suffrage, secret ballot, payment for MPs, equal electoral districts), explain why these demands emerged in the industrial context, and identify at least one long-term change Chartism contributed to.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the political exclusion of the working class from representation in the 1830s; the specific demands of the Charter and the reasoning behind each; the Chartist campaign — petitions, demonstrations, the three petition drives and their rejection; why Chartism declined (emigration of leaders, economic improvement, partial reform); the long-term legacy — most Chartist demands were eventually implemented (secret ballot 1872, universal male suffrage 1918); examine Chartism as an example of working-class political agency in the industrial period.
wider: Compare Chartism with contemporary working-class political movements — trade unionism, socialist parties — examining what Chartism achieved by political means that unions addressed industrially
Examine Chartism's connections to Australia — William Cuffay transported to Tasmania; British Chartists on Victorian goldfields — tracing how radical political ideas travelled with migrants

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe Chartism as a failure because its petitions were rejected without understanding the longer-term influence — most of its demands were eventually enacted. Making the short-term/long-term distinction explicit (building on K15's temporal framework) prevents oversimplification.

success_criteria: Describes the People's Charter's main demands and explains why they emerged in the industrial context
Identifies changes that Chartism contributed to, including long-term legacy

nodes.label: The French Revolution — causes, impacts and the spread of new political ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the causes and impacts of the French Revolution on politics and citizens' rights, including its effects in Britain and the USA.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the main causes of the French Revolution (inequality, Enlightenment ideas, financial crisis, weak monarchy) and identify at least two political impacts (e.g. declaration of rights, spread of republican ideas, Napoleonic reforms).
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the social conditions of pre-revolutionary France; the Enlightenment ideas (Rousseau, Voltaire, Locke) that challenged inherited authority; the fiscal crisis and Estates-General; the Revolution's phases — 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man, constitutional monarchy, Republic, Terror, Directory, Napoleon; the Napoleonic Code's legal reforms; how the Revolution spread the ideas of popular sovereignty, equality before the law, and national self-determination; the reaction in Britain (Burke vs Paine) and the USA (enthusiastic reception of republican ideals); the longer-term effects on European political thought and nationalist movements.
wider: Examine the contrast between Burke's conservative critique and Paine's radical defence of the French Revolution — as a case study in how the same events were interpreted through different value frameworks
Trace how the French Revolution's ideas influenced nationalist movements elsewhere — Latin American independence, Italian Risorgimento, 1848 revolutions across Europe

response_modes.reason: Students commonly focus on the dramatic events of the Revolution (the Terror, executions) without understanding its ideological significance — that it demonstrated popular sovereignty was possible, and its ideas spread beyond France. Multiple examples of impact across different countries build this picture.

success_criteria: Describes main causes of the French Revolution and its key political impacts
Explains how the Revolution's ideas affected political thinking in at least one other country

nodes.label: Religious belief and social reform — the role of faith in abolition, labour rights and women's rights
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the role of religious beliefs in the movement to end the slave trade, in reforms improving industrialisation's negative effects, in the enfranchisement of women, and in the rise of organised labour.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the role of religious belief in at least two of the four reform areas and explain why religious conviction motivated reform in each case.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the Evangelical and Quaker role in abolition (Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect, the Society of Friends); the role of the Social Gospel movement in labour reform; the role of temperance and Methodist Christianity in women's suffrage campaigns (Christian Women's Temperance Union in Australia); Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891) as a Catholic response to socialism and capitalism defending workers' rights; explain why religious conviction motivated reform — belief in human dignity, equality before God, social responsibility; examine the tension between religious conservatism (defending existing social order) and religious radicalism (challenging inequality in God's name).
wider: Examine how religious reformers and secular radicals sometimes allied and sometimes conflicted in the same reform movements — what did they share and where did they diverge?
Investigate a specific religious reformer in depth — Wilberforce, Florence Nightingale, or Pope Leo XIII — examining how religious conviction shaped their approach and what they achieved

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat religious belief and social reform as separate historical domains. Examining how faith motivated specific reform campaigns — not as incidental background but as the driving conviction — builds a more complex understanding of how change happened.

success_criteria: Describes the role of religious belief in at least two reform movements with specific examples
Explains why religious conviction motivated reform — what theological or moral basis underpinned each case
